content: Residual activity of insecticides can be assessed by conducting weekly tests on treated surfaces until the 24-hour mortality rate falls below 80%. For residual treatment evaluations in passenger cabins, small pieces of non-permeable plastic sheeting are affixed to the interior walls, and six WHO cones are placed on the sheeting. Ten non-blood-fed female mosquitoes, aged 2–5 days, are introduced into each cone for 30 minutes. After exposure, the mosquitoes are transferred into clean, individually marked holding cups containing a 10% sugar solution on cotton wool. These cups are maintained at 27°C ± 2°C and 80% ± 10% relative humidity for 24 hours. Mortality is recorded after this period. If the control group mortality exceeds 20%, the test is invalidated. For cargo holds, which predominantly consist of a single material, fewer WHO cones are required compared to passenger cabins. A minimum of six cones are placed in different locations within the hold, including one on each wall and two on the ceiling. Control bioassays are conducted in the same locations and with the same number of cones prior to treatment to ensure no residues are present. Residual activity is measured weekly until the 24-hour mortality rate is below 80%. Post-treatment controls are performed by affixing non-permeable plastic sheeting to predefined wall locations and placing six WHO cones on the sheeting. The same mosquito exposure and observation protocol is followed as described for passenger cabins. The WHO currently recommends three methods for aircraft disinsection: blocks away, preflight and top-of-descent spraying, and residual treatment. Preflight spraying involves applying an aerosol insecticide with rapid action and limited residual effect to the flight deck, passenger cabin (including toilets, overhead lockers, and crew rest areas), and other areas. This is done by ground staff before passengers board, but not more than one hour before the doors are closed. The application rate is 35 grams of formulation per 100 cubic meters, with a droplet size of 10–15 µm. Blocks away spraying is conducted by crew members after passengers have boarded and the cabin doors are closed, but before takeoff. An aerosol insecticide with rapid action is used, and the air-conditioning system is turned off during spraying. The flight deck is sprayed before the pilot boards, and overhead luggage rack doors are closed only after spraying is complete. Cargo holds are also disinsected. Top-of-descent spraying is performed as the aircraft begins its descent to the arrival airport. WHO recommends using an aerosol containing 2% d-phenothrin, applied with the air recirculation system set from high to normal flow. Residual spraying involves treating the internal surfaces of the passenger cabin and cargo hold (excluding food preparation areas) with a compression sprayer equipped with a constant flow valve and flat fan nozzle, as per WHO specifications. The insecticide is applied at 2 g/m² at intervals not exceeding two months. The emulsion is applied at 10 mL/m² to prevent runoff. Residual sprays are applied by professional pest control operators to ensure long-term residual activity on aircraft interior surfaces. In electrically sensitive areas, aerosol application may be necessary instead of compression spraying. For equipment decontamination, the following steps are recommended: wash with hot soapy water to remove oil and residue, rinse thoroughly, and dry. Rinse in a 1–5% acetic acid solution, followed by two consecutive technical acetone baths, and dry. Bake in an oven for 24 hours at approximately 150°C. Glassware can be baked for a shorter time at a higher temperature. Used wash solutions should be disposed of properly. Acetic acid solutions should be changed every other day if equipment is washed daily, or freshly mixed for sporadic washing. Acetone can be used longer and replaced as needed. Testing chambers should be constructed with smooth internal wall panels made of stainless steel, aluminum, glass, or other suitable materials for easy cleaning of insecticide or solvent residues. The chamber should have a tight-fitting entrance door, fluorescent lighting, and an exhaust fan to remove insecticide vapor after each test. Hooks are installed in the ceiling corners to suspend test cages. A fan is placed on the chamber floor for air circulation.
